items.item: Without a unique_key, an incremental model defaults to append-only behavior, inserting every row regardless of duplicates.

at.step: Reveal: SCD policy and the merge

items.item: With a unique_key, a row present in both the new and old data gets updated in place instead of appended as a duplicate.

at.step: Reveal: SCD policy and the merge

items.item: MERGE provides a single statement that can conditionally INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE rows.
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE names the clause that detects a target row with no matching source row.
A deleted source row is invisible to a plain incremental extract unless the design is told to look for one.
A changed row merges by a stated unique key, or it silently becomes a duplicate.

items.item: The crossover is a number, computed from the shop's own constants, not a feeling about which approach sounds more modern.
A slow incremental load produces staleness that eventually catches up; a deleted-row gap never closes on its own.

at.step: Predict: which risk did the design not name?

items.item: A table already past its own crossover needs the crossover recomputed from its current numbers, not a switch made by feel.

at.step: Prove it: a table well past its own crossover

items.item: A fact landing before its dimension gets an inferred placeholder key, backfilled once the real dimension arrives, rather than being dropped.
This topic leaves out dimensional-modelling mechanics, SCD implementations, merge syntax, dbt incremental models, CDC itself, the semantic-layer products, and orchestration of the loads.
Grain-first dimensional modelling and incremental merge loads are established practice, not an emerging technique.
This topic gives the shop its warehouse design; the next design is CDC from the transactional database into the lakehouse, the cleanest source of changed rows.
Not every requested mart earns its keep, and revenue is defined once in a semantic layer rather than recomputed per mart.
